findings.title: Chinese national arrested in Milan after US issues arrest warrant for Hafnium attacks
findings.summary_md: Italian police arrested Xu Zewei, a 33-year-old from Shanghai, at Milan's airport on July 3, 2025, on a US warrant charging wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and unauthorized access to protected computers. The Justice Department unsealed a nine-count indictment accusing Xu and co-defendant Zhang Yu of computer intrusions from February 2020 to June 2021, including the Hafnium campaign that compromised thousands of computers worldwide. Prosecutors said Xu acted at the behest of China's Ministry of State Security and the Shanghai State Security Bureau, and that the team targeted a Texas university in 2020 to obtain COVID-19 vaccine research.

findings.title: Patents by Silk Typhoon-linked company shed light on Beijing's offensive hacking capabilities
findings.summary_md: SentinelLabs researcher Dakota Cary mapped Justice Department indictments to Shanghai Firetech, a company the DOJ said works on behalf of the Shanghai State Security Bureau and took part in Silk Typhoon attacks while previously being identified in the 2021 Hafnium campaign. The review found patents for offensive tooling, including home-appliance analysis and evidence collection software that could support surveillance of individuals abroad. Cary concluded the company serves offensive missions beyond the Hafnium cluster.

findings.title: Italy extradites alleged Chinese state hacker to US
findings.summary_md: Xu Zewei was extradited from Milan to the United States in late April 2026 and held at the Houston Federal Detention Center, his lawyer confirmed. Xu has denied involvement in Chinese government hacking, claiming mistaken identity, and was on vacation in Milan when arrested in July 2025. China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian criticized the Italian government's decision at a press conference the following Monday.

findings.title: US posts $10 million reward for accused Chinese 'Hafnium' hacker
findings.summary_md: The State Department's Rewards for Justice program offered up to $10 million for information on the whereabouts of Zhang Yu, identified as director of Shanghai Firetech Information Science and Technology and accused of acting for the Chinese government in breaches of thousands of computers. The announcement says Zhang violated the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act in attacks on at least one university and a law firm, alongside Xu Zewei, who was extradited to the US in April. Zhang remains at large.
